sourcedFrom: BANISH 556 PRODUCT MANUAL — ABSENT — no revision, date code or edition statement printed anywhere in the document. (ABSENT — no copyright line printed.)
cleanIntro: The BANISH 556 is a 3D-printed Inconel core in a stainless blast chamber, and BANISH states plainly that it is not designed to be fully disassembled — the baffles do not come out. The only part you take off is the mount adapter. That makes the whole of its service a soak, a brass brush down the blast chamber and a thorough thread clean, on a 500 to 600 round interval. It is a dedicated 5.56 NATO / .223 REM can, full-auto rated with no barrel length restriction, and it ships with a 1/2x28 direct-thread adapter into an industry-standard 1.375x24 HUB rear thread. Everything about unloading your host rifle comes from that rifle's own manual.

steps.title: Host unloaded, action open and visibly clear
steps.action: Before the can comes off, the rifle has to be unloaded with the action open and visibly empty of ammunition. BANISH does not print a clearing procedure for your host and does not pretend to — it sends you to the firearm's own manual or to a licensed dealer if you are unsure. An AR-15's clearing drill is not an SBR's is not a bolt gun's, and only that gun's book covers yours.
steps.prose: Suppressed guns are quiet, and quiet makes people casual. Treat it exactly as you would the unsuppressed rifle.
steps.quote: Before removing the suppressor from the host firearm, be sure the firearm is unloaded, and the action is open, so it is visibly clear of any ammunition.
steps.cite: BANISH 556 PRODUCT MANUAL — ABSENT — no revision, date code or edition statement printed anywhere in the document. — Warning, p.2
steps.warn: If you are at all unsure as to the proper procedures to ensure that your firearm is unloaded, please consult your firearm user’s manual/instructions and/or contact a properly licensed dealer or the manufacturer of your firearm.

steps.title: BANISH 556 caliber ceiling — 5.56 NATO / .223 REM
steps.action: Confirm what the can has been living on. The BANISH 556 is a dedicated 5.56 NATO / .223 REM suppressor and that is its entire caliber range — it is not a multi-caliber .30 can with a 5.56 tuning. Solid lead and plated lead bullets are also outside what BANISH recommends through it, which rules out most cheap plinking .223 cast loads.
steps.prose: Where it is unusually permissive is barrel length and rate of fire: it is full-auto rated with no barrel length restriction, so a 10.5 inch AR is inside the envelope.
steps.caution: The use of solid lead or plated lead bullets is not recommended.
steps.cite: BANISH 556 PRODUCT MANUAL — ABSENT — no revision, date code or edition statement printed anywhere in the document. — Specs, p.3

steps.title: Let it cool before you touch it
steps.action: The can will be very hot during and after firing. Wait for it to cool, or use a suppressor cover or gloves, before you put a hand on it to unscrew it. A hot direct-thread can that you grab and twist is the classic way to take skin off, and it is also the moment people over-torque a joint that only ever needed to be hand tight.
steps.prose: Inconel holds heat a long time after the rifle has stopped feeling warm. Give it longer than you think.
steps.quote: When removing the suppressor, use extreme caution as it may be hot to the touch after firing. Use a suppressor cover (sold separately) or gloves to avoid burns or other injuries.
steps.cite: BANISH 556 PRODUCT MANUAL — ABSENT — no revision, date code or edition statement printed anywhere in the document. — Warning, p.2
steps.warn: Hot after firing. Cover or gloves.

steps.title: Unscrew the can off the barrel
steps.action: With the rifle clear and the can cool, unscrew the suppressor anticlockwise off the barrel threads. It went on hand tight and it comes off the same way; nothing here needs a wrench. If it is stubborn, it is fouling on the threads rather than a torqued joint, and forcing it is how a 1/2-28 thread gets damaged.
steps.prose: Direct-thread cans loosen under fire, which is why BANISH asks you to check tightness after 5 rounds and every 30 thereafter. A can that has been walking will often come off very easily.
steps.aside: We recommend checking the security of the attachment after 5 discharges of the firearm and every 30 discharges thereafter.
steps.quote: Hand tighten suppressor only. Once snug, it is ready for use.
steps.cite: BANISH 556 PRODUCT MANUAL — ABSENT — no revision, date code or edition statement printed anywhere in the document. — Mounting the Suppressor (Direct Thread), p.4

steps.title: Mount adapter out of the back — and that is as far as it opens
steps.action: Take the mounting adapter out of the rear of the suppressor. This is the ONLY part of a BANISH 556 that comes off. The baffles are additive-manufactured as one piece with the core and cannot be removed, so there is no stack to pull, no end cap to unscrew and no tool to buy. Anyone telling you to open one further is describing a different can.
steps.prose: The rear thread under the adapter is the 1.375x24 HUB interface, which is why a direct-thread or QD adapter can be swapped in its place.
steps.quote: The additive-manufactured BANISH 556 is not designed to be fully disassembled, and its baffles cannot be removed. Only the mount interface can be removed for cleaning.
steps.cite: BANISH 556 PRODUCT MANUAL — ABSENT — no revision, date code or edition statement printed anywhere in the document. — Cleaning, p.6

steps.title: Thread protector on the muzzle while the can is off
steps.action: With the suppressor off, fit a thread protector or another muzzle device to the barrel. Exposed muzzle threads on a rifle that lives in a case get dinged, and a bruised thread crest is what cross-threads the can next time — which is the exact chain BANISH warns leads to a baffle strike. It also protects the crown, which is what your accuracy actually rests on.
steps.prose: This is a storage and transport habit, not a cleaning step, and it costs nothing.
steps.quote: Once the suppressor is removed from the host firearm, BANISH recommends using a thread protector or other muzzle device to protect the muzzle threads and crown during storage or transport.
steps.cite: BANISH 556 PRODUCT MANUAL — ABSENT — no revision, date code or edition statement printed anywhere in the document. — Warning, p.2

steps.title: Twenty-four hour soak, then a brass brush
steps.action: Submerge the whole suppressor in cleaning solution, or seal the muzzle end and fill it, and leave it for 24 hours. Mild firearm solvents, sonic wash solutions and even dish soap all work; what does not is anything that will strip the Cerakote. Once it has soaked, take a brass brush to the blast chamber — that is where the hard carbon lives on a 5.56 can.
steps.prose: The interval is every 500 to 600 rounds. A gas gun's back pressure rises as the can loads up, so letting it drift makes the rifle itself run dirtier.
steps.quote: To clean, submerge the entire suppressor in cleaning solution. Or, seal the muzzle end of the suppressor and fill its interior with cleaning solution. In both cases, let the suppressor soak for 24 hours.
steps.cite: BANISH 556 PRODUCT MANUAL — ABSENT — no revision, date code or edition statement printed anywhere in the document. — Cleaning, p.6
steps.warn: Be sure not to use solutions that will strip the Cerakote finish.

steps.title: Threads — all of them, inside and out
steps.action: With the mounting adapter out, clean every thread on the assembly: the suppressor's own rear HUB threads, the adapter's internal and external threads, and the barrel threads on the rifle. BANISH calls this out specifically because a HUB can lives or dies on those two joints seating square, and carbon in a 1.375x24 thread is what puts the bore off axis.
steps.prose: If a crush washer sits under an existing muzzle brake, it has to come out before a suppressor goes on that barrel — a crush washer cannot index a can.
steps.caution: If a crush washer is used with an existing muzzle brake, it must be removed prior to suppressor mounting.
steps.quote: Remove the mounting adapter and thoroughly clean the threads, removing any debris or buildup. This includes the suppressor’s threads, as well as all internal and external mounting threads.
steps.cite: BANISH 556 PRODUCT MANUAL — ABSENT — no revision, date code or edition statement printed anywhere in the document. — Cleaning, p.6

steps.title: Field strip complete
steps.action: The can is off the rifle and the mount adapter is out of the back. That is the entire published strip for a BANISH 556 — the baffles stay where they are. Dry it fully, reinstall the adapter, hand tighten it back onto a clean barrel and fire 10 to 15 clearing rounds on the next range trip to blow out whatever the soak loosened.
steps.prose: There is no Deep Clean to walk on this one, because BANISH publishes no procedure that goes further than the mount interface.
steps.quote: Once clean, allow the suppressor to dry. Reinstall mounting adapters and reattach to the firearm.
steps.cite: BANISH 556 PRODUCT MANUAL — ABSENT — no revision, date code or edition statement printed anywhere in the document. — Cleaning, p.6

deepAbsentReason: BANISH publishes NO deeper procedure for the BANISH 556, and says why in its own words: 'The additive-manufactured BANISH 556 is not designed to be fully disassembled, and its baffles cannot be removed. Only the mount interface can be removed for cleaning.' (Cleaning, p.6). The core and baffle set are 3D-printed as one Inconel piece, so there is physically nothing to take apart beyond the mount adapter, which the field strip already covers. The warranty page reinforces it — 'Suppressors built using additive manufacturing processes cannot be repaired.' (p.7). Inventing a baffle-stack teardown for this can would be substitution from a different product.

cleaning.name: INTERIOR
tasks: Submerge the whole can, or seal the muzzle end and fill it, and soak 24 hours
Mild firearm solvent, sonic wash solution or dish soap — nothing that strips Cerakote
Brass brush the blast chamber once it has soaked
Do NOT attempt to remove the baffles — they are not removable

cleaning.name: MOUNT & THREADS
tasks: Remove the mounting adapter — the only removable part
Clean the suppressor's rear HUB threads (1.375x24)
Clean the adapter's internal AND external threads
Clean the barrel threads on the host; remove any crush washer under an existing brake

cleaning.name: AFTER CLEANING
tasks: Let it dry fully before the adapter goes back in
Fire 10-15 clearing rounds at the next session to evacuate loosened debris
Fit a thread protector to the bare muzzle whenever the can is off

reassembly: Dry the suppressor completely, then reinstall the mounting adapter into the rear HUB thread.
Check the barrel threads and the adapter face are clean and undamaged.
Line the threaded end up with the barrel and start it by hand, taking care not to cross-thread.
Screw it down until the mount seats firmly against the barrel shoulder — hand tight only, no tools.
Confirm there is no visible gap between the barrel shoulder and the face of the suppressor mount.
Fire 10-15 clearing rounds at the next range session to evacuate anything the soak loosened.
fncheck: Check the fit before you fire it: on a direct-thread mount there must be NO visible gap between the barrel shoulder and the face of the suppressor mount, and the can must be free of any obstruction down the bore. If there is any gap, do not fire the host with the suppressor attached — a can that is not seated against the thread shoulder gives poor accuracy and can damage the product. Once shooting, re-check that it is still securely tightened after the first 5 discharges and every 30 thereafter, letting it cool or using a cover before you re-tighten.
